questions.stem: A 47-year-old client with type 2 diabetes managed with metformin is admitted with acute cholecystitis. Pain began 18 hours ago after a fried-food dinner. Which admission findings require follow-up by the nurse? Select all that apply.
options: BP 136/84 mm Hg
T 38.8 °C (101.8 °F) with chills overnight
SpO₂ 97% on room air
WBC 15,400/mm³ with 11% bands
Creatinine 0.8 mg/dL
Random blood glucose 246 mg/dL
optionRationales: This BP is within an acceptable range and does not signal a systemic or circulatory problem.
Correct. A temperature above 38.5 °C (101.3 °F) is a systemic sign on the course cutoffs; the gallbladder inflammation is no longer only local.
An SpO₂ of 97% on room air shows adequate oxygenation.
Correct. A WBC above 12,000/mm³ with increased bands (a left shift) shows the bone marrow is releasing young neutrophils, a systemic, acute bacterial-type response.
Creatinine is within the reference range, so kidney function is not a current concern.
Correct. The stress of inflammation raises blood glucose, and in a client with diabetes this value needs follow-up (the client is also NPO, so metformin will be held and glucose checked as ordered).
questions.rationale: This item links three parts of the module. The fever and the high WBC with bands meet the slide cutoffs for systemic inflammation, so the local gallbladder problem has spread its effects to the whole body. The same stress response raises blood glucose, which matters in a client with diabetes who will be NPO with metformin held. BP, SpO₂, and creatinine are normal and are reassuring baseline data.
questions.takeaway: Compare each value with the systemic cutoffs and with the client's history: fever, WBC/bands, and a stress-related glucose rise all need follow-up.
questions.hintContent: Recall the systemic cutoffs (T, HR, RR, WBC/bands), what a left shift means, and how the stress of inflammation affects blood glucose in diabetes.
questions.hintStrategy: Sort each option as normal or abnormal first, then ask whether the abnormal value is clinically significant for this client's history.

questions.stem: A client with acute cholecystitis has the following findings. Which findings are LOCAL manifestations of the inflamed gallbladder rather than signs of a systemic response? Select all that apply.
options: Right upper quadrant (RUQ) tenderness to palpation
T 38.8 °C (101.8 °F) with chills
Guarding, with the client stopping inhalation when the RUQ is pressed
WBC 15,400/mm³ with 11% bands
Thickened, edematous gallbladder wall on ultrasound
Fatigue and loss of appetite
optionRationales: Correct. Tenderness over the organ is local pain (dolor), caused by bradykinin and prostaglandins plus pressure from swelling.
Fever with chills is a systemic sign; mediators have reached the brain's temperature center.
Correct. Guarding and stopping inhalation protect the inflamed organ; this is local pain with impaired function (functio laesa).
A high WBC with bands comes from the bone marrow and is a systemic finding.
Correct. Increased capillary permeability lets fluid leak into the gallbladder wall; this is local swelling (tumor) seen on imaging.
Fatigue and loss of appetite are whole-body (systemic) effects of circulating mediators.
questions.rationale: For an internal organ, the classic signs show up as tenderness, guarding, and swelling of that organ. Each has a mechanism: permeability causes the edematous wall, and mediators plus pressure cause pain and loss of function. Fever, chills, a high WBC with bands, fatigue, and poor appetite are systemic because mediators have spread into the bloodstream. Sorting local from systemic findings tells the nurse whether the response is still contained.
questions.takeaway: Local = cardinal signs at the organ (tenderness, guarding, edema); systemic = fever, WBC/bands, fatigue, anorexia.
questions.hintContent: Connect the five cardinal signs and their causes to how they appear in an internal organ, and recall the list of systemic findings.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option ask: is this happening at the gallbladder itself, or is the whole body reacting?

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · What Inflammation Is (and Isn't)
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client reports RUQ pain that began 18 hours ago after a fatty meal. Findings: RUQ tenderness with guarding, T 38.8 °C (101.8 °F), HR 108, WBC 15,400/mm³ with 11% bands, and an ultrasound showing an inflamed gallbladder wall. Which statement best describes the client's condition?
options: Acute gallbladder inflammation that remains localized to the RUQ
Acute gallbladder inflammation that has produced a systemic response
Chronic, lymphocyte-driven gallbladder inflammation limited to the RUQ
An IgE-mediated allergic reaction to the meal with systemic effects
optionRationales: The fever, tachycardia, and high WBC with bands meet the systemic cutoffs, so the response is not limited to the RUQ.
Correct. Rapid onset over hours with neutrophil-driven labs fits acute inflammation, and T >38.5 °C, HR >90, and WBC >12,000 with bands show a systemic response.
Onset over hours with a neutrophil/band response points to acute, not chronic, inflammation, and the findings are not limited to the RUQ.
An allergic reaction would cause hives, wheezing, or airway swelling within minutes, not organ tenderness and a left shift 18 hours later.
questions.rationale: Two judgments are combined. First, acute versus chronic: onset over hours, classic local signs, and a neutrophil response with bands indicate acute inflammation. Second, local versus systemic: fever above 38.5 °C, HR above 90, and WBC above 12,000 with bands meet the course cutoffs for a systemic response. Together these describe acute cholecystitis with systemic effects.
questions.takeaway: Hours-long onset + bands = acute; T >38.5 °C, HR >90, WBC >12,000 = systemic.
questions.hintContent: Compare acute and chronic inflammation (onset, main cells) and apply the systemic-sign cutoffs from the assessment slide.
questions.hintStrategy: Decide acute vs. chronic first, then local vs. systemic, and pick the option that gets both right.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client with acute cholecystitis and type 2 diabetes (usually takes metformin) is admitted to await cholecystectomy tomorrow. T 38.6 °C (101.5 °F), HR 104, pain 8/10. Prescriptions include NPO, IV fluids, IV morphine PRN, and capillary glucose checks with correction insulin. Which interventions should the nurse include in the preoperative plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Maintain NPO status and explain that eating makes the gallbladder contract
Offer a small low-fat snack once the nausea improves
Check capillary glucose as prescribed and give correction insulin
Hold the morphine until the surgeon examines the client so pain is not masked
Give the usual morning metformin with a sip of water
Monitor temperature, heart rate, and respiratory rate for worsening
optionRationales: Correct. Food triggers cholecystokinin release and gallbladder contraction, which increases pain and inflammation; NPO rests the organ and prepares for anesthesia.
Any food makes the inflamed gallbladder contract and breaks the NPO order before surgery.
Correct. The stress of inflammation raises glucose, and the client is NPO with metformin held, so glucose monitoring and correction insulin are needed.
Withholding analgesia "so it won't mask symptoms" is outdated; prescribed pain medication is given and the client is reassessed.
Oral diabetes drugs are held as prescribed while the client is NPO before surgery.
Correct. The client already shows systemic signs; rising T, HR, or RR would mean the inflammation is worsening.
questions.rationale: The preoperative plan combines resting the inflamed organ (NPO, because food causes gallbladder contraction), managing the effect of inflammation on a chronic condition (stress hyperglycemia in diabetes while NPO with metformin held), and watching the systemic signs already present. Pain is treated as prescribed rather than withheld.
questions.takeaway: Before surgery for an inflamed organ: NPO to rest it, treat pain, manage glucose in diabetes, and trend the systemic signs.
questions.hintContent: Link why NPO rests the gallbladder, how inflammation and NPO status affect glucose and diabetes medicines, and which vital signs show systemic spread.
questions.hintStrategy: Test each option against the orders and against the reason behind it; eliminate anything that feeds the gallbladder or is an outdated practice.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: Four hours after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy, a client rates incisional pain 7/10, takes shallow breaths, and says, "It hurts too much to breathe deeply or get up." Lung bases are slightly diminished. T 37.8 °C (100.0 °F), HR 94, SpO₂ 95%. The last IV morphine was given 4 hours ago. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Coach the client to use the incentive spirometer now
Help the client walk in the hallway right away
Give the prescribed PRN IV morphine and reassess
Report the temperature to the surgeon as a systemic sign
optionRationales: Deep breathing is the goal, but the client cannot breathe deeply while pain is 7/10; the spirometer is coached after the analgesic takes effect.
Walking is important but will not happen with uncontrolled pain; it follows pain relief.
Correct. Pain is blocking deep breathing and walking; treating it first lets the client take part in the measures that prevent complications.
A temperature of 37.8 °C is below the course cutoff of 38.5 °C for a systemic sign; the findings do not need an urgent report.
questions.rationale: The client needs deep breathing and walking, but pain is the barrier. The prescribed opioid is for severe pain; it does not treat inflammation but allows recovery to proceed. The mildly elevated temperature and slightly high HR do not meet the systemic cutoffs, so there is no reason to call the surgeon before treating pain. Once pain is controlled, the nurse coaches the incentive spirometer and ambulation.
questions.takeaway: When pain blocks recovery activities, give the prescribed analgesic first, then coach.
questions.hintContent: Connect the role of opioids after surgery, why deep breathing and walking matter, and the course cutoff for a systemic temperature.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask what is stopping the client from doing the helpful actions; remove that barrier first.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: On postoperative day 1 after cholecystectomy for acute cholecystitis, a client has T 37.1 °C (98.8 °F), HR 80, WBC 9,100/mm³ with 4% bands, and CRP 2.9 mg/dL (8.2 mg/dL on admission). Port sites are clean and dry. The client says, "Now that my gallbladder is gone, I'll go right back to fast-food lunches every day." Which finding is the priority for the nurse to address before discharge?
options: CRP of 2.9 mg/dL, which is still above the reference range
WBC of 9,100/mm³ with bands down to 4%
Clean, dry port-site incisions with edges approximated
The client's plan to resume daily fast-food lunches
optionRationales: CRP falls quickly when inflammation resolves; a drop from 8.2 to 2.9 mg/dL shows improvement, and it is expected to keep falling.
A normal WBC with normal bands shows the systemic response has resolved.
Clean, dry, approximated port sites are expected healing findings.
Correct. A Western diet high in fast food promotes inflammation and conflicts with an anti-inflammatory, higher-fiber, lower-fat pattern; this knowledge gap needs teaching before discharge.
questions.rationale: Evaluating outcomes means judging each finding. The falling CRP, normal WBC and bands, and normal vital signs show the inflammation is resolving, and the incisions look healthy. The remaining problem is the client's plan to eat fast food daily, a modifiable risk factor for inflammation, so diet teaching is the priority before discharge.
questions.takeaway: A falling CRP and normalized WBC show recovery; an unhealthy diet plan is a teaching need.
questions.hintContent: Recall how CRP and WBC/bands change as inflammation resolves, and which dietary pattern promotes inflammation.
questions.hintStrategy: Mark each option as improving/expected or as a problem; the priority is the one that is still a problem.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: 1000: A 68-year-old female client with rheumatoid arthritis is admitted with weakness and dizziness when standing. For 4 months she has taken naproxen 500 mg PO twice daily and adds over-the-counter ibuprofen 'when my joints are bad.' Reports 'black, sticky stools' for 2 days and a burning pain in the upper abdomen. Skin pale and cool. Alert and oriented ×4.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. Which actions should the nurse take at this time? Select all that apply.
options: Hold the NSAIDs and notify the provider
Teach the client to take the naproxen with milk
Use fall precautions and help the client get up slowly
Replace the naproxen with aspirin for the joint pain
Monitor hemoglobin, blood pressure, and heart rate
Attribute the weakness to an RA flare because the ESR is elevated
optionRationales: Correct. Black stools, epigastric burning, a falling hemoglobin, and orthostatic changes point to an NSAID-related upper GI bleed; the drugs are held and the provider notified.
Taking an NSAID with food or milk is preventive teaching; it does not address an active bleed.
Correct. Orthostatic hypotension and dizziness from blood loss create a high fall risk.
Aspirin also blocks protective prostaglandins and impairs platelets, so it would worsen the bleeding.
Correct. Trending hemoglobin and vital signs shows whether the bleeding and volume loss are continuing.
The ESR has been about the same for months, reflecting her chronic RA; the new weakness is explained by blood loss, not a flare.
questions.rationale: NSAIDs block prostaglandins everywhere, including those that protect the stomach lining, and taking two NSAIDs together doubles the risk. The drop in hemoglobin from 12.8 to 8.9 g/dL, tachycardia, and orthostatic hypotension show significant blood loss. The stable, mildly elevated ESR reflects her long-standing chronic inflammation and does not explain the acute change. Priorities are stopping the cause, preventing falls, and monitoring for ongoing bleeding.
questions.takeaway: Black stools + falling Hgb + orthostatic changes on NSAIDs = GI bleed: hold, notify, prevent falls, monitor.
questions.hintContent: Connect the protective role of prostaglandins, the meaning of the hemoglobin and vital-sign trends, and what a stable ESR in chronic RA represents.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the acute problem from the trends first, then choose actions that stop the cause and keep the client safe.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: 1030: An 84-year-old client is admitted from a long-term care facility. The client's daughter says the client has been 'not herself' since yesterday: more confused, refused breakfast, and slid to the floor while getting up (no injury). Baseline: oriented to person and place, walks with a walker. Now oriented to person only and picking at the bed linens. Weak, moist cough. Crackles in the right lower lobe.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. The nurse recognizes that this older adult's infection is presenting atypically. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Apply oxygen as prescribed to keep SpO₂ at or above 92%
Obtain blood and sputum cultures before the first antibiotic
Compare the client's orientation with the facility baseline
Collect a urine specimen for culture to look for a source
optionRationales: Correct. An SpO₂ of 89% with RR 26 is a breathing problem, and hypoxia can worsen confusion; oxygenation comes first.
Cultures are important before antibiotics, but they do not come before correcting hypoxia.
The change from baseline is already documented; re-comparing does not treat the low oxygen level.
The crackles point to the lungs as the source, and a urine specimen does not address the immediate hypoxia.
questions.rationale: In older adults, infection often shows up as new confusion, falls, and poor appetite, with only a small temperature rise over a low baseline (here 1.3 °C). The HR >90, RR >20, and WBC >12,000 with bands show a systemic response. Among the actions, the SpO₂ of 89% is the most immediate threat (breathing), so oxygen is applied first; cultures and further work-up follow.
questions.takeaway: Atypical infection in older adults: compare with baseline to recognize it, but treat ABC problems like hypoxia first.
questions.hintContent: Link atypical signs of infection in older adults, the systemic-sign cutoffs, and the ABC priority framework.
questions.hintStrategy: Several options are appropriate; pick the one that addresses the airway/breathing threat.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 64-year-old client's lower-leg wound was left open to heal by secondary intention after an abscess was drained 12 days ago. Which findings indicate the wound is NOT progressing through the reparative phase as expected? Select all that apply.
options: Most of the wound bed is beefy red, moist, and granular
An area of pale, gray, friable tissue at the lower edge
Moderate thick, tan-green drainage on the dressing
A foul odor that persists after cleansing
T 37.2 °C (99.0 °F) with a WBC in the normal range
Pain rising from 2/10 to 7/10 over the past 24 hours
optionRationales: Beefy red, moist granulation tissue is the expected sign of healthy repair.
Correct. Pale, gray, friable tissue is unhealthy and shows repair has stalled in that area.
Correct. Thick, colored drainage is purulent exudate, suggesting infection.
Correct. A persistent foul odor after cleansing suggests infection or dead tissue.
A normal temperature and WBC are not signs of stalled healing, but they also do not rule out a local wound infection.
Correct. Pain should decrease as repair progresses; a sharp rise suggests infection.
questions.rationale: In the reparative phase, the wound should show beefy red granulation, decreasing serous drainage, shrinking size, and lessening pain. Gray friable tissue, purulent drainage, persistent odor, and rising pain point to infection or impaired healing. Systemic markers can stay normal while a local infection develops, so local findings must be reported on their own.
questions.takeaway: Local wound signs (gray tissue, purulent drainage, odor, rising pain) need reporting even when temperature and WBC are normal.
questions.hintContent: Recall what healthy granulation and healthy exudate look like, and whether normal systemic findings rule out a local infection.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option, ask whether it describes the expected reparative-phase picture; anything that departs from it is selected.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: An 18-month-old admitted with pneumonia has had vomiting and poor oral intake for 2 days. Which finding requires the nurse's immediate follow-up?
options: Temperature of 38.9 °C (102.0 °F) 20 minutes after acetaminophen
Respiratory rate of 36/min with SpO₂ 95% on 1 L of oxygen
Capillary refill of 4 seconds and no wet diaper in 8 hours
Fussy and crying with tears during the assessment
optionRationales: Fever is an expected systemic sign of the lung inflammation, and the antipyretic has had little time to work. It needs monitoring but is not the most urgent finding.
A fast respiratory rate is expected with fever and pneumonia in a toddler, and the SpO₂ is acceptable on the prescribed oxygen.

Correct. Capillary refill over about 3 seconds and no wet diaper for many hours show the skin and kidneys are not being perfused. After 2 days of vomiting and poor intake, this signals significant fluid loss that needs action and reporting now.
A fussy child who cries with tears is alert and still producing tears, which is reassuring about mental status and hydration.
questions.rationale: Children lose fluid faster than adults because their total fluid volume is smaller and their kidneys conserve water poorly. The best bedside checks of fluid balance in a young child are mental status, capillary refill, and wet diapers. Fever and fast breathing are expected systemic signs of pneumonia, but delayed capillary refill with no urine output for 8 hours shows poor perfusion and requires immediate follow-up.
questions.takeaway: In a young child, check mental status, capillary refill, and wet diapers to spot dangerous fluid loss.
questions.hintContent: Connect the expected systemic signs of pneumonia with why fluid losses are more dangerous in toddlers and which bedside checks show poor perfusion.
questions.hintStrategy: Separate findings expected from the illness from the one showing that tissues and kidneys are not being perfused.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A client has painful, red, warm skin on both shoulders after a day at the beach without sunscreen. T is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F), and the skin is intact. The client asks, "Why is it red and hot, and do I need an antibiotic?" Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "Bacteria multiplied in the heat; an antibiotic will stop the redness."
"The sun injured the skin, and widened vessels cause the redness; no antibiotic is needed."
"Your immune system has started attacking your own skin cells, so you will need a steroid."
"Fluid leaking from vessels is starting an infection, so an antibiotic is a good idea."
optionRationales: Sunburn is caused by UV radiation, a physical agent, not by bacteria; antibiotics would not help.
Correct. UV radiation is a physical agent that injures cells, and vasodilation brings more warm blood to the area, causing redness and heat. No microorganism is involved.
Sunburn is not an autoimmune process; the response is to an external injury.
Leaking fluid causes swelling, not infection; with intact skin and no fever, there is no sign of infection.
questions.rationale: Inflammation is a response to any harm, and infection is only one cause. UV radiation is a physical agent. The redness and heat of the sunburn come from vasodilation bringing extra warm blood to the injured skin. Because no microorganism is present, an antibiotic has no role.
questions.takeaway: Inflammation is not infection: physical injuries like sunburn cause redness and heat through vasodilation, without germs.
questions.hintContent: Recall the three categories of causes of inflammation and the process that produces redness and heat.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the response that correctly identifies both the cause and the mechanism.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client with a sprained right wrist has had a cloth-wrapped cold pack applied for 20 minutes every 2–3 hours, with the wrist elevated, for 24 hours. Which finding best indicates these measures are achieving the intended effect?
options: The skin over the wrist stays pale and cool 1 hour after the pack is removed
The client reports numbness in the fingers while the cold pack is in place
Wrist circumference has decreased from 18.5 cm to 17.6 cm
Bruising over the wrist has spread toward the forearm
optionRationales: Skin that stays pale and cool long after cold removal suggests impaired circulation or cold injury, not success.
Numbness during cold therapy means the cold should be removed; it is an adverse effect.
Correct. Cold causes vasoconstriction and elevation lowers hydrostatic pressure, both reducing leakage; a measurable decrease in circumference proves less edema.
Spreading bruising shows worsening, not improvement.
questions.rationale: Swelling comes from increased capillary permeability and higher hydrostatic pressure. Cold (vasoconstriction) and elevation (lower hydrostatic pressure, better venous and lymph return) target those mechanisms. The best evidence they worked is a measurable drop in circumference at the same spot. Pale, cool, or numb skin signals harm from the treatment.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate swelling with an objective measurement such as circumference.
questions.hintContent: Connect why cold and elevation reduce swelling with how to measure a change in swelling and the safety signs of cold therapy.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for the option that is both objective and shows the intended effect, not an adverse effect.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client reports a painful, swollen left knee after kneeling on a hard floor for several hours. Which technique should the nurse use to determine whether the knee has increased warmth?
options: Compare both knees using the back of the hand
Palpate the left knee firmly with the fingertips
Measure the knee's skin with a tympanic thermometer
Ask the client whether the knee feels warm
optionRationales: Correct. The back of the hand is most sensitive to temperature, and the other knee serves as the client's own normal.
Fingertips are less sensitive to temperature, and firm pressure adds pain without improving accuracy.
A tympanic thermometer measures core temperature in the ear, not local skin warmth.
The client's report is subjective and not an accurate assessment of warmth.
questions.rationale: Local warmth (calor) comes from vasodilation bringing warm core blood to the site. It is assessed with the dorsal surface of the hand, comparing the affected area with the same spot on the opposite side.
questions.takeaway: Check warmth with the back of the hand and compare sides.
questions.hintContent: Think about which part of the hand senses temperature best and what the comparison standard should be.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that are subjective or measure the wrong thing.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client who had a myocardial infarction 5 days ago asks, "Once the inflammation settles down, will my heart muscle grow back?" Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: "Yes, heart muscle fully regenerates within 6 to 8 weeks with rest."
"New muscle cells from your bone marrow will replace the damaged area."
"It will regenerate if you take an anti-inflammatory medicine daily."
"The damaged area heals as scar tissue, which does not pump."
optionRationales: Heart muscle has limited regeneration; rest does not make it regrow.
Bone marrow regenerates its own cells but does not replace heart muscle.
Anti-inflammatory drugs reduce inflammation but cannot make heart muscle regenerate.
Correct. Muscle, including heart muscle, has limited regeneration, so the damaged area heals by scar (cicatrix), which is less functional.
questions.rationale: In the reparative phase, tissues that divide often (skin, GI and respiratory lining, bone, marrow, lymphoid) regenerate. Nervous, muscle (including cardiac), and elastic tissue have limited regeneration and heal by scar, which is strong but does not contract.
questions.takeaway: Heart muscle and nerve tissue heal by scar, not regeneration.
questions.hintContent: Recall which tissues regenerate quickly and which have limited regeneration.
questions.hintStrategy: Classify heart muscle, then choose the outcome that matches its regeneration ability.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client recovering from drainage of a thigh abscess has a wound that is now filling with beefy red, moist tissue. The client asks for a between-meal snack. Which snack should the nurse recommend to best support this phase of healing?
options: A bowl of buttered white rice with gravy
Saltine crackers with a diet soda
Greek yogurt with sliced strawberries
A glass of apple juice and a rice cake
optionRationales: White rice with gravy provides mostly carbohydrate and fat, with little protein or vitamin C.
Saltines and diet soda provide little protein, vitamin C, or useful fluid for repair.
Correct. Greek yogurt provides protein and strawberries provide vitamin C, both needed to build granulation tissue and collagen.
Apple juice and a rice cake are mostly simple carbohydrate, low in protein and vitamin C.
questions.rationale: Beefy red, moist tissue is granulation tissue, which means the wound is in the reparative stage. Fibroblasts now lay down collagen, which needs protein for building blocks and vitamin C to form strong fibers. The best snack supplies both.
questions.takeaway: Granulation = reparative phase; support it with protein plus vitamin C.
questions.hintContent: Identify the stage from the wound description, then recall which nutrients build new tissue and collagen.
questions.hintStrategy: Name the stage first, then pick the snack with the nutrients that stage needs.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client with pneumonia has T 38.9 °C (102.0 °F) and HR 104/min, is sweating heavily, and has taken only 300 mL of oral fluid today. Acetaminophen was given 30 minutes ago. Which nursing action is the priority?
options: Encourage oral fluids and change the damp gown and linens
Restrict oral fluids to 1 L per day to avoid fluid overload
Add heavy blankets so the client can sweat out the fever
Give a second antipyretic dose now to speed the drop in fever
optionRationales: Correct. Fever and sweating increase fluid loss, and fluids support repair; dry linens promote comfort while the antipyretic takes effect.
Restricting fluids worsens the deficit caused by fever and sweating.
Heavy blankets trap heat and raise the temperature further.
The antipyretic was just given; repeating it early risks toxicity, and the temperature is rechecked after it has had time to work.
questions.rationale: The fever and tachycardia are systemic signs of the lung inflammation. Prostaglandins drive the fever, and acetaminophen has just been given to lower it. While it takes effect, the nurse replaces the fluid lost through fever and sweating and provides comfort. Fluids are also part of promoting healing.
questions.takeaway: Fever care: give the prescribed antipyretic, replace fluids, keep the client dry, and recheck.
questions.hintContent: Connect systemic signs, how an antipyretic works and is timed, and why fever increases fluid needs.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that worsen the fluid deficit, trap heat, or repeat a drug too soon.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client at 32 weeks' gestation has a BP of 152/98 mm Hg and 2+ proteinuria and is being monitored for preeclampsia, an inflammation-mediated disorder of the blood vessel lining. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider immediately?
options: Mild swelling of both ankles that improves after a night's rest
Severe headache with spots in the vision despite acetaminophen
Needing to urinate more often than before the pregnancy began
A dull lower back ache after standing at work for several hours
optionRationales: Mild dependent ankle swelling that resolves with rest is common in pregnancy.
Correct. A severe headache with visual changes is a severe feature, showing the disorder is affecting the brain.
Urinary frequency is a common, expected change of pregnancy.
A dull back ache after standing is a common discomfort of pregnancy.
questions.rationale: Preeclampsia is an inflammation-mediated hypertensive disorder that damages the lining of blood vessels and stresses organs. A severe headache or visual disturbance signals progression to severe disease and must be reported immediately; the other findings are common pregnancy changes.
questions.takeaway: Preeclampsia + severe headache or visual changes = report immediately.
questions.hintContent: Recall how preeclampsia affects blood vessels and organs and which symptoms show progression.
questions.hintStrategy: Separate common pregnancy discomforts from a sign of organ involvement.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The RN is caring for an 88-year-old client admitted with pneumonia whose baseline temperature is 36.1 °C (97.0 °F). Which instruction is most important for the RN to give the unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP)?
options: Report the temperature only if it rises above 39 °C (102.2 °F)
Keep the client in bed to conserve energy and do not offer to walk
Report any new confusion or change in behavior right away
Limit the client's fluids to 1 L per day to prevent fluid overload
optionRationales: Older adults often have a blunted fever response; waiting for 39 °C could miss worsening infection, and a low temperature can also be significant.
Strict bed rest increases complications; activity is individualized, not withheld.
Correct. New confusion is often the first sign of worsening infection in an older adult, and the UAP can observe and report it.
Fluids are not restricted without a prescription; fever and infection increase fluid needs.
questions.rationale: Older adults may show infection as confusion, falls, or poor appetite instead of a high fever, and a temperature below 36 °C also counts as a systemic sign. The UAP can observe and report changes, while the RN assesses and acts. The most useful instruction targets the earliest, most likely warning sign in this age group.
questions.takeaway: Teach the UAP to report new confusion in older adults right away.
questions.hintContent: Link atypical signs of infection in older adults, the systemic temperature cutoffs (high and low), and what the UAP may observe and report.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the instruction within UAP scope that catches the earliest sign of trouble for this age group.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the admitting diagnoses of clients in an urgent care clinic. Which clients have inflammation that is NOT caused by a microorganism? Select all that apply.
options: A client with sunburn after a day at the beach
A client with strep throat and a positive rapid antigen test
A client with a chemical burn from a drain cleaner
A client with an ankle sprain from a fall
A client with a urinary tract infection from E. coli
A client with contact dermatitis from poison ivy
optionRationales: Correct. UV radiation is a physical agent.
Strep throat is caused by bacteria, a microorganism.
Correct. Drain cleaner is an external chemical agent.
Correct. Trauma is a physical agent.
E. coli is a bacterium, a microorganism.
Correct. Poison ivy oil is a chemical agent.
questions.rationale: Inflammation is triggered by microorganisms, chemical agents, or physical agents. Sunburn and sprain are physical; drain-cleaner burn and poison ivy dermatitis are chemical. Strep throat and an E. coli UTI are caused by bacteria.
questions.takeaway: Inflammation can occur with no infection: physical and chemical agents cause it too.
questions.hintContent: Recall the three categories of causes of inflammation and examples of each.
questions.hintStrategy: Label each client microorganism, chemical, or physical, then select the non-microbial ones.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client sprained the right wrist in a fall 2 hours ago. The wrist is red, warm, and swollen, and there is no wound. Which interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Elevate the wrist above the level of the heart
Apply a cold pack wrapped in a thin towel for 15–20 minutes
Apply a heating pad on high while the client sleeps
Massage the wrist firmly to move the swelling
Wrap the wrist tightly with an elastic bandage overnight
Check capillary refill and sensation in the fingers
optionRationales: Correct. Elevation lowers capillary hydrostatic pressure and helps fluid drain back, reducing swelling.
Correct. Cold causes vasoconstriction, limiting leakage and numbing pain; the barrier and time limit prevent cold injury.
Heat causes vasodilation and increases swelling in a fresh injury, and high heat during sleep risks burns.
Firm massage pushes fluid and can worsen the injury.
A tight wrap left on overnight can cut off circulation as swelling increases.
Correct. Swelling can compress vessels and nerves; checking circulation and sensation below the injury detects this early.
questions.rationale: The redness and warmth come from vasodilation, and the swelling from increased permeability and hydrostatic pressure. Cold and elevation work directly against these mechanisms in the first 24–48 hours, and neurovascular checks catch the danger of swelling compressing vessels. Heat, massage, and tight overnight wraps increase swelling or cause harm.
questions.takeaway: Fresh sprain: elevate, wrapped cold 15–20 minutes, and check circulation and sensation.
questions.hintContent: Connect the causes of redness and swelling with how cold, heat, and elevation affect blood vessels.
questions.hintStrategy: Select actions that reduce blood flow or pressure at the site and keep the limb safe; reject anything that increases them.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse is assessing incisions for several clients on postoperative day 3. Which findings should the nurse report to the provider? Select all that apply.
options: A small amount of thin, pale pink drainage, less than on day 1
Thick, yellow-green drainage with a foul odor
A sudden increase in bright red drainage saturating the dressing
Narrow pink edges a few millimeters wide along a closed incision
Cloudy, tan drainage with redness spreading beyond the incision
Scant serous drainage at the edge of the dressing
optionRationales: Serosanguineous drainage that is decreasing is expected early healing.
Correct. Thick, colored, foul drainage is purulent exudate, suggesting infection.
Correct. A sudden increase in bright red drainage suggests bleeding and needs a prompt report.
A narrow band of pink at the edges is expected local inflammation during healing.
Correct. Cloudy drainage with spreading redness suggests a spreading infection.
Scant serous drainage is expected and reflects normal exudate.
questions.rationale: Exudate is expected in Stage 2 and should move from sanguineous to serosanguineous to serous while decreasing. A narrow pink edge along a closed incision is normal local inflammation. Purulent drainage, sudden bright red bleeding, and redness spreading beyond the incision are departures from the expected pattern and must be reported.
questions.takeaway: Decreasing serous/serosanguineous drainage and narrow pink edges are expected; purulent, bright red, or spreading findings are reported.
questions.hintContent: Recall the exudate types and the healthy drainage trend, plus what normal inflammation at an incision looks like.
questions.hintStrategy: Classify each finding as expected healing or a warning sign using type, trend, and spread.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Acute vs. Chronic Inflammation
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 34-year-old client has had Crohn's disease for 8 years. During the nursing interview, which findings should the nurse recognize as effects of long-standing chronic inflammation? Select all that apply.
options: Fatigue that persists despite adequate sleep
Loss of appetite that has lasted for months
Sudden fever of 40 °C (104 °F) with rigors starting today
Unintentional weight loss of 5 kg (11 lb) over 6 months
Complete resolution of symptoms within 3 days
Symptoms that have persisted and flared over many years
optionRationales: Correct. Persistent fatigue is a common whole-body effect of chronic inflammation and is one of the interview questions on the assessment slide.
Correct. Months of poor appetite reflect ongoing inflammation and reduce the nutrients needed for repair.
A sudden high fever with rigors suggests a new acute process, such as an infection, that needs prompt reporting.
Correct. Gradual weight loss reflects the long-term effects of chronic inflammation on appetite and nutrient use.
Resolution within days fits acute, not chronic, inflammation.
Correct. Persisting and flaring over years is the pattern of chronic inflammation.
questions.rationale: Chronic inflammation lasts months to years, and circulating mediators cause fatigue, loss of appetite, and weight loss. Asking about fatigue and appetite is part of the inflammation-focused interview. A sudden high fever with rigors or resolution within days points to an acute process instead.
questions.takeaway: Chronic inflammation = persistent fatigue, poor appetite, gradual weight loss, and flares over years.
questions.hintContent: Compare the time course and whole-body effects of chronic versus acute inflammation, and recall what the interview asks about.
questions.hintStrategy: Select findings that are gradual and long-lasting; reject sudden or short-lived ones.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 5-year-old is admitted with a deep-tissue infection of the thigh that requires IV antibiotics and imaging. Which interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Calculate each medication dose using the child's weight in kilograms
Request a child life specialist to prepare the child for procedures through play
Offer aspirin for fever and discomfort
Monitor urine output and the number of voids
Choose invasive imaging even when a noninvasive option would work
optionRationales: Correct. Pediatric doses are calculated by weight in kilograms.
Correct. Child life support and play therapy help children cope with procedures.
Aspirin is avoided in children because of the risk of Reye syndrome with viral illness; other antipyretics are used as prescribed.
Correct. Children lose fluid quickly and have immature kidneys, so output is an early measure of fluid balance.
Noninvasive imaging is preferred for children when it can answer the question.
questions.rationale: Pediatric care considerations on the slides include child life support, play therapy, and noninvasive imaging. Children's smaller fluid volume and immature kidneys make output monitoring important, and doses are weight-based. Aspirin is avoided in children because of Reye syndrome.
questions.takeaway: Pediatric inflammation care: weight-based dosing, play/child life, output monitoring, noninvasive imaging, no aspirin.
questions.hintContent: Connect the pediatric care considerations and fluid risks with the aspirin warning for children.
questions.hintStrategy: Check each option against what is safe and developmentally appropriate for a young child.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: An 83-year-old client is on postoperative day 3 after hip fracture repair. The client's baseline temperature is 36.2 °C (97.2 °F). Which findings could indicate a developing infection? Select all that apply.
options: New inattention and disorientation to time
Eating 30% of meals, down from 80% yesterday
Incisional pain of 3/10 with movement
Oriented to person, place, and time, as at admission
Decreasing serosanguineous drainage on the dressing
optionRationales: Correct. New confusion is often the first sign of infection in older adults.
Correct. Although below the usual fever cutoff, this is more than 1 °C above the client's baseline, which is significant in an older adult.
Correct. A sudden drop in appetite is an atypical sign of infection in older adults.
Mild pain with movement is expected on postoperative day 3.
Orientation unchanged from admission is reassuring.
Serosanguineous drainage that is decreasing is the expected exudate pattern after surgery.
questions.rationale: Older adults have a blunted fever response, so findings are compared with the client's own baseline. A rise of about 1 °C over baseline, new confusion, and poor appetite can signal infection. Decreasing serosanguineous drainage and mild pain fit normal healing.
questions.takeaway: In older adults, compare with baseline: new confusion, poor appetite, or a small temperature rise can mean infection.
questions.hintContent: Link atypical infection signs in older adults with expected postoperative healing findings and drainage patterns.
questions.hintStrategy: Compare each finding with the client's own baseline and with what normal healing looks like on day 3.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client is admitted with acute pancreatitis. Which findings indicate a systemic (generalized) inflammatory response according to the course cutoffs? Select all that apply.
options: Epigastric tenderness to palpation
Heart rate 96/min
Respiratory rate 18/min
WBC 15,200/mm³
Guarding of the upper abdomen
optionRationales: Tenderness over the pancreas is a local finding.
Correct. A temperature above 38.5 °C (101.3 °F) is a systemic sign.
Correct. A heart rate above 90/min is a systemic sign.
A respiratory rate of 18/min does not exceed the cutoff of 20/min.
Correct. A WBC above 12,000/mm³ is a systemic sign.
Guarding protects the inflamed organ and is a local finding.
questions.rationale: The course lists systemic signs as T >38.5 °C or <36 °C, HR >90, RR >20, and WBC >12,000 or increased bands. Tenderness and guarding are local signs at the pancreas. Applying the exact cutoffs separates systemic findings from normal values like an RR of 18.
questions.takeaway: Systemic cutoffs: T >38.5 °C or <36 °C, HR >90, RR >20, WBC >12,000 or ↑ bands.
questions.hintContent: Recall the four systemic-sign cutoffs and the difference between local and systemic findings.
questions.hintStrategy: Check each numeric value against its cutoff; treat organ tenderness and guarding as local.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to apply a cold pack to a client's ankle, which was sprained 2 hours ago and is swollen and warm. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Wrap the cold pack in a thin cloth barrier
Elevate the ankle on pillows above the level of the heart
Set a timer so the pack stays on for 15–20 minutes
Assess skin integrity, sensation, and circulation
optionRationales: A cloth barrier is needed but comes after the baseline assessment.
Elevation reduces swelling but follows the baseline assessment.
Timing the application is part of the procedure after assessment.
Correct. A baseline check of skin, sensation, and circulation is needed before cold is applied, both to detect compression from swelling and to compare after treatment.
questions.rationale: Swelling from increased permeability can compress vessels and nerves, and cold itself can injure skin. The nurse first assesses skin, sensation, and circulation to establish a baseline, then wraps the pack, elevates, and applies it for 15–20 minutes.
questions.takeaway: Assess skin, sensation, and circulation before applying cold.
questions.hintContent: Connect the risks of swelling and cold therapy with the steps of safe cold application.
questions.hintStrategy: When all options are correct steps, choose the assessment that must come before the others.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client with bacterial pneumonia has a fever and chest discomfort and is receiving an IV antibiotic. The client asks how the prescribed ibuprofen will help. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: "It kills the bacteria that injured the lung, working alongside the antibiotic."
"It blocks prostaglandins, which cause vasodilation, pain, and fever."
"It stops mast cells from releasing histamine and heparin."
"It blocks leukotrienes, which are the main cause of the fever."
optionRationales: NSAIDs do not kill bacteria; the antibiotic treats the cause.
Correct. Ibuprofen blocks prostaglandin production, reducing fever (thermostat reset) and pain.
NSAIDs do not block histamine release from mast cells.
Leukotrienes attract WBCs; prostaglandins cause fever.
questions.rationale: The antibiotic treats the bacterial cause, while ibuprofen treats the symptoms. Prostaglandins produced at the site cause vasodilation, pain, and fever by acting on the hypothalamus. NSAIDs lower prostaglandin production, so pain and fever fall.
questions.takeaway: Antibiotics treat the cause; NSAIDs block prostaglandins to relieve pain and fever.
questions.hintContent: Match each mediator to its main effect and recall what NSAIDs do and do not do.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify which mediator causes fever, then pick the drug action that targets it.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The nurse receives handoff on four clients with inflammatory conditions. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client who just received IV penicillin and reports throat tightness and a hoarse voice
A client with leg cellulitis who has a new red streak up the thigh and HR 112/min
A client with rheumatoid arthritis and 90 minutes of morning stiffness who asks for a scheduled medication
A client with a sprained ankle who asks for a fresh ice pack
optionRationales: Correct. Throat tightness and hoarseness after a drug signal airway swelling from possible anaphylaxis, an airway threat.
Spreading redness with tachycardia shows the infection is spreading and becoming systemic; this client is seen next.
Morning stiffness is an expected finding of chronic RA and is stable.
A comfort need for a stable local injury is the lowest priority.
questions.rationale: Prioritize with ABCs and then "systemic before local, unstable before stable." Possible anaphylaxis threatens the airway and comes first. Spreading cellulitis with tachycardia is next. Stable chronic RA symptoms and a local comfort request follow.
questions.takeaway: Airway threat from overactive inflammation first, then spreading/systemic, then chronic stable, then local comfort.
questions.hintContent: Connect signs of anaphylaxis, signs of spreading or systemic inflammation, and the expected picture of chronic inflammation.
questions.hintStrategy: Apply ABCs first, then rank remaining clients by stability.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: The nurse is following a client's deep leg laceration from the day of injury through healing. Which finding indicates the wound has entered the reparative phase?
options: Redness and warmth around the wound within the first hour
Neutrophils adhering to capillary walls near the wound
Beefy red, moist tissue filling the wound bed
Thin, straw-colored fluid collecting on the dressing
optionRationales: Redness and warmth are cardinal signs of vasodilation in Stage 1.
Neutrophil adhesion is part of the cellular response in Stage 1.
Correct. Granulation tissue filling the wound is Stage 3, the reparative phase.
Serous exudate is characteristic of Stage 2.
questions.rationale: Stage 1 includes vasodilation (the redness and warmth of the cardinal signs) and the cellular response. Stage 2 is exudate production. Stage 3 is repair, marked by granulation tissue and later scar.
questions.takeaway: Redness/warmth and WBC adhesion = Stage 1; serous fluid = Stage 2; granulation = Stage 3.
questions.hintContent: Link the cardinal signs to the vascular stage and recall what each stage looks like at the wound.
questions.hintStrategy: Assign each option to a stage, then choose the one in the reparative phase.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing findings for several clients. Which findings are mainly caused by histamine and heparin? Select all that apply.
options: A raised, itchy wheal within minutes of a mosquito bite
Neutrophils and macrophages gathering in an infected cut
Fever and body aches during influenza
Blood that keeps flowing at an injured site instead of clotting
Pain and fever that are relieved by ibuprofen
Itching and hives that are relieved by an antihistamine
optionRationales: Correct. Mast cells release histamine within seconds, causing local vasodilation, leak, and itching.
Leukotrienes attract neutrophils and macrophages to the site.
Prostaglandins cause fever and aches.
Correct. Heparin, released with histamine, prevents clotting and keeps blood flowing to the site.
Findings relieved by an NSAID are driven by prostaglandins.
Correct. An antihistamine blocks histamine, so relief of itching and hives confirms histamine caused them.
questions.rationale: Histamine and heparin are released from mast cells: histamine increases blood flow and permeability and causes itching and hives, and heparin prevents clotting. Which drug relieves a symptom also points to the mediator: antihistamines work on histamine effects, while NSAIDs work on prostaglandin effects.
questions.takeaway: Histamine = itch, hives, leak (relieved by antihistamines); heparin = no clotting; prostaglandins = fever and pain (relieved by NSAIDs).
questions.hintContent: Match each mediator to its signature effect and to the drug class that blocks it.
questions.hintStrategy: Name the mediator behind each finding, using the relieving drug as a clue.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for a 15-year-old with Crohn's disease, a chronic inflammatory condition, who is below the expected height for age. Which action should the nurse include in the plan of care?
options: Encourage skipping meals on school days to reduce diarrhea
Recommend aspirin for joint pain during flares
Discuss body image and school only with the parent present
Refer to a dietitian for a high-calorie meal plan
optionRationales: Skipping meals worsens the nutritional deficit that is slowing growth.
Aspirin is avoided in children and teens (Reye syndrome risk) and irritates the GI tract.
Adolescents should be asked privately about body image and school.
Correct. Chronic gut inflammation decreases absorption and slows growth; a dietitian provides nutrient-dense, high-calorie meals as part of collaborative care.
questions.rationale: Chronic inflammation of the gut reduces nutrient absorption, which affects a child's growth, weight, and strength. The dietitian is a key collaborative team member for chronic inflammation. Height and weight are plotted on a growth chart, and adolescents are interviewed privately.
questions.takeaway: Child with chronic gut inflammation and poor growth: dietitian referral and growth monitoring.
questions.hintContent: Connect the effect of chronic gut inflammation on growth with the collaborative team and adolescent care.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that worsen nutrition, are unsafe for teens, or ignore adolescent privacy.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client has an acutely swollen, warm left knee after a fall 3 hours ago. There is no wound. The client asks how elevating the leg above heart level will reduce the swelling. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: "It lowers pressure in the capillaries so leaked fluid can drain back."
"It raises arterial pressure in the leg to push the extra fluid out of the joint."
"It increases blood flow to the knee to speed up healing."
"It stimulates histamine release to tighten the capillaries."
optionRationales: Correct. Elevation lowers capillary hydrostatic pressure and lets gravity help fluid return through veins and lymph vessels.
Elevation does not raise arterial pressure, and higher pressure would push more fluid out.
More blood flow would increase swelling; that is the effect of heat, not elevation.
Histamine widens and loosens capillaries; it does not tighten them.
questions.rationale: In the vascular stage, vasodilation raises capillary hydrostatic pressure and increased permeability lets plasma leak out, causing swelling. Elevation lowers that pressure and uses gravity to help fluid return, which is why it is an independent intervention for acute swelling.
questions.takeaway: Elevation reduces swelling by lowering capillary hydrostatic pressure and aiding venous and lymph return.
questions.hintContent: Recall what causes swelling in the vascular stage and how gravity and pressure affect fluid movement.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the explanation that reverses the mechanism that caused the swelling.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 64-year-old client with a 40 pack-year smoking history has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), with a daily productive cough and dyspnea that has slowly worsened over 6 years. Which intervention is the nurse's priority to slow the progression of the chronic airway inflammation?
options: Teach the client to complete a 7-day course of antibiotics
Support the client in quitting smoking
Recommend a daily NSAID to reduce airway inflammation
Restrict daily fluid intake to reduce mucus production
optionRationales: Antibiotics treat acute infections on top of COPD but do not stop the chronic process.
Correct. Cigarette smoke is the persistent irritant that keeps the chronic inflammation going; removing it (a modifiable risk factor) slows progression.
Long-term daily NSAIDs carry GI, kidney, and bleeding risks and do not remove the cause.
Restricting fluids thickens secretions and does not affect the inflammation.
questions.rationale: Chronic inflammation persists when the trigger keeps returning. In COPD, cigarette smoke restarts the response every day. Prevention equals avoidance of triggers, and smoking is a modifiable risk factor, so smoking cessation is the most effective intervention. Antibiotics and NSAIDs do not remove the cause.
questions.takeaway: Chronic inflammation from a persistent irritant: remove the trigger.
questions.hintContent: Connect why chronic inflammation persists with modifiable risk factors and the limits of drug therapy.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask what keeps the inflammation going, then choose the action that removes it.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Nursing Assessment and Diagnostic Tests
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client with seasonal allergic rhinitis who takes cetirizine 10 mg daily is scheduled for allergy skin-prick testing next week. Which instruction should the nurse give?
options: "Take an extra dose of cetirizine the night before the test."
"Take your usual cetirizine dose the morning of the test."
"Double the cetirizine dose for 3 days before the test to be safe."
"Stop the cetirizine several days before the test as directed."
optionRationales: An extra dose would block the skin reaction even more.
Taking the antihistamine on test day blocks the wheal-and-flare response.
Doubling the dose increases the chance of a false-negative result.
Correct. Antihistamines block histamine, the mediator that produces the wheal and flare, so they are stopped beforehand to avoid false negatives.
questions.rationale: Skin testing identifies allergens by exposing the skin to them and watching for a histamine-driven wheal and flare. Because antihistamines block histamine, they must be stopped for several days as the allergist directs, or the test may be falsely negative.
questions.takeaway: Hold antihistamines before skin testing; they block the histamine wheal.
questions.hintContent: Link the mediator that causes the skin-test wheal with how antihistamines work.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask how the drug would change the test result, then choose the instruction that keeps the result accurate.
